title: Agent Card and discovery
summary: The Agent Card is a JSON document that an A2A server publishes to describe its identity, endpoints, capabilities, skills and security. Clients fetch it from a well-known URL, a registry or direct configuration.
useIf: You publish an agent for others to call, or you must decide how a client finds and trusts a remote agent.
avoidIf: You treat the card as proof of identity or as a contract: it is a claim that must be verified and then authenticated against.

explain.md: A server serves its card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` (the well-known URI pattern of RFC 8615) [[r6]] [[tr3]]. In v1.0 the required fields are `name`, `description`, `supportedInterfaces`, `version`, `capabilities`, `defaultInputModes`, `defaultOutputModes` and `skills` [[r1]]. Each entry in `supportedInterfaces` has a `url`, a `protocolBinding` (`JSONRPC`, `GRPC` or `HTTP+JSON`), a `protocolVersion` and an optional `tenant`. The list is ordered and the first entry is preferred.

explain.caption: Read each field as a claim and decide what to check [[r1]]
head: Field
What it declares
Check before calling
rows: Pick a binding you support, send `tenant` exactly as declared
A missing or false flag means the operation returns `UnsupportedOperationError`
Descriptive only, not a contract: test the skill
API key, HTTP, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, mutual TLS
Obtain credentials out of band, then authenticate every request
Proves origin and integrity of the card, nothing about behaviour

explain.title: Finding and vetting a card
explain.alt: Flow from needing an agent, through a known URL or a registry query, to fetching the card, verifying it, choosing an interface and authenticating.
explain.src:
flowchart TD
  N[Need an agent] --> K{Know the host?}
  K -->|yes| W[GET well-known card]
  K -->|no| R[Query registry]
  W --> V[Verify card and capabilities]
  R --> V
  V --> I[Pick first supported interface]
  I --> A[Authenticate every request]

explain.md: Cards may be signed as a JWS (RFC 7515) over the RFC 8785 canonical form, excluding the `signatures` field [[r1]] [[r18]] [[r19]]. Servers SHOULD send `Cache-Control: max-age` and an `ETag`, and clients SHOULD use conditional requests [[r6]]. The spec defines no registry API, so you design that layer yourself [[r6]]. Anything sensitive belongs in the authenticated **extended card** (`GetExtendedAgentCard`, declared by `capabilities.extendedAgentCard`), not the public one.

explain.title: Foundry differs from the default path
explain.md: A Foundry agent's card requires Microsoft Entra authentication and uses the path `agentCard/v1.0`, not `/.well-known/agent-card.json`. Anonymous card access is not supported (checked 2026-10-13) [[r17]].

whereToUse: A public agent that publishes its card at a well-known URL for open discovery
An enterprise catalog where a registry stores cards and filters them by skill or tag
A client library that resolves a card, picks an interface and builds an agent object from it
A security review that checks which schemes, scopes and interfaces a callee declares
A gateway that caches cards and refreshes them with conditional requests

use: Well-known URI for agents meant for broad discovery on a domain you can reach
A curated registry when many teams publish agents and you need governance and skill search
Direct configuration for a few tightly coupled, high-trust agents
avoid: Do not put internal URLs or sensitive skills in a public card
Do not follow a card's endpoint blindly when tasks will carry sensitive data
Do not skip the capability check: operations the card does not declare fail
flips: Cards change weekly: honor `Cache-Control` and `ETag` and refresh with conditional requests instead of pinning forever
Cards carry sensitive detail: authenticate the card endpoint and serve an extended card or selective disclosure
Trust is low and data is sensitive: pin the host and verify the JWS signature against a key you trust

pitfalls.symptom: Calls fail with `UnsupportedOperationError` on streaming or the extended card
pitfalls.cause: The client assumed a capability the card does not declare
pitfalls.fix: Read `capabilities` first and fall back to polling when `streaming` is false or missing [[r1]]

pitfalls.symptom: Traffic flows to an unexpected host after a card refresh
pitfalls.cause: The client trusted the `url` in a refreshed card without any allowlist or signature check
pitfalls.fix: Allowlist hosts, verify the JWS when present and alert when an interface URL changes

pitfalls.symptom: Internal URLs and sensitive skills show up in a public card
pitfalls.cause: Everything was placed in the unauthenticated card
pitfalls.fix: Keep the public card minimal and serve detail through the authenticated extended card [[r6]]

pitfalls.symptom: Requests are rejected on a shared multi-agent endpoint
pitfalls.cause: The `tenant` value declared on the interface was not sent
pitfalls.fix: Send `tenant` exactly as declared on the selected interface [[r1]]

scenarios.title: Forty internal agents, one platform team
scenarios.situation: Forty agents owned by different teams must be findable by skill. Security wants an audit of who can see which agent. Cards change about weekly.
constraints: Search by skill and audit needed
unknowns: Is there a platform team to run a catalog?
Do some agents hide sensitive skills?
scenarios.question: How do clients discover agents?

options.name: Curated registry with authenticated access and selective disclosure
options.why: Central governance, search by skill, per-caller visibility and one place to audit.
options.tradeoff: You build and operate the registry, since the spec defines no registry API.

options.name: Well-known URI scan across team domains
options.why: Standard and automatable, and each team stays in control of its card.
options.tradeoff: No central search or policy, and every endpoint needs its own protection.

options.name: Hard-coded endpoints in each client
options.why: Every card change forces client redeployments across forty agents.
options.tradeoff: Right for two tightly coupled agents that rarely change.

flips.if: Only five agents and one owning team

flips.then: Add signed cards and host pinning.

scenarios.takeaway: Many owners and a need to search mean a registry.

scenarios.title: A third-party agent that will see customer data
scenarios.situation: Your assistant will send customer records to an external agent found through a partner directory. A wrong endpoint would leak data. The card changes roughly monthly.
unknowns: Does the partner sign its cards?
scenarios.question: How much do you trust the card at runtime?

options.name: Pin host and key, verify the JWS, alert on interface changes
options.why: A card refresh cannot silently redirect customer data, and signatures prove the card's origin.
options.tradeoff: Key rotation and change approval take operational effort.

options.name: Fetch the well-known card on every call and follow it
options.tradeoff: Whoever controls DNS or the host controls where data goes.

options.name: Follow any card URL the model discovers
options.why: A prompt-injected or malicious card could redirect tasks and data anywhere.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only in a sandbox with synthetic data.

flips.if: Data is public and low risk
flips.then: Fetch with caching and skip pinning.
Pin the host and TLS identity and review each card change by hand.

scenarios.takeaway: The card is a claim. Pin what you cannot afford to be wrong about.

quiz.q: Put the steps of using a remote agent in a sensible order.
items: Check capabilities and the supported interfaces
Select the first interface whose binding you support
Obtain credentials out of band for the declared scheme
Send the authenticated request, with `tenant` if declared
quiz.explain: You learn what the agent supports before choosing an interface, and credentials depend on the declared scheme. Authentication still happens on every request, not once at discovery.

quiz.q: Which fields are required in a v1.0 Agent Card? Select all that apply.
quiz.explain: `supportedInterfaces` and `skills` are required, along with name, description, version, capabilities and the default input and output modes. `provider` and `signatures` are optional.

quiz.q: A card carries a valid JWS signature. What does that prove?
options: The agent is safe to send sensitive data to
The listed skills behave as described
The card was published by the key holder and was not modified
The agent will accept any credential
quiz.explain: A signature establishes origin and integrity of the card document. It says nothing about the agent's behaviour, safety or authentication policy.

flashcards.front: Where does an A2A server publish its Agent Card by default?
flashcards.back: At `/.well-known/agent-card.json` on its domain. Foundry agents use an authenticated custom path, `agentCard/v1.0`.

flashcards.front: Which Agent Card fields tell a client which operations are available?
flashcards.back: `capabilities` (`streaming`, `pushNotifications`, `extensions`, `extendedAgentCard`). A missing flag means the operation returns `UnsupportedOperationError`.

flashcards.front: How is an Agent Card signed?
flashcards.back: As a JWS (RFC 7515) over the RFC 8785 canonical form of the card, excluding the `signatures` field.

flashcards.front: Where should sensitive card detail live?
flashcards.back: In the authenticated extended card (`GetExtendedAgentCard`), not the public card.
